fields.title: Day 29 — Pray for Everyone
fields.body_html:
“First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone—for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity. This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

— 1 Timothy 2:1–4 (BSB)

Who do you usually pray for? Probably yourself, your family, maybe your friends. Those are great things to pray about!

But Paul says to pray for “everyone.” That’s a big list!

Paul mentions a few specific kinds of prayer. Petitions and prayers mean asking God for things. Intercessions means praying on behalf of someone else, standing in the gap for them before God. And thanksgiving means thanking God for people.

Then Paul says to pray “for kings and all those in authority.” That means leaders: presidents, prime ministers, governors, mayors, judges, police officers, principals and teachers. When Paul wrote this, the rulers of the Roman Empire weren’t friendly to Christians. Some were cruel. But Paul still said to pray for them!

Why? Because God is in charge of the whole world, and He can work through leaders to bring peace. And because God cares about leaders’ souls too.

Look at the end of the passage. God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” God loves every single person in the world. He wants all of them to know Jesus. When we pray for everyone, we’re praying with God’s own heart.

That means we can pray for:

  • Leaders in our country and around the world.
  • Missionaries who are telling people about Jesus in other places.
  • People who don’t know Jesus yet, including friends, neighbors and family members.
  • Countries where Christians are persecuted for their faith.
  • People going through disasters, wars or hard times you hear about in the news.
  • People you don’t like! (Remember Day 17.)

You might not be able to travel around the world. But through prayer, you can help people all over the globe. Prayer is like a superpower that lets a kid in their bedroom make a difference on the other side of the planet.

Think about it: Who is someone you’ve never prayed for before, but should? What about a leader, a missionary or a country?

Try this: Make a prayer list with five categories: a leader, a missionary, a country, someone who doesn’t know Jesus, and someone who’s having a hard time. Pray through it today.

Dear God, thank You that You love every person in the world and want everyone to be saved. I pray for [name a leader], for missionaries around the world, for [name a country], and for people who don’t know You yet, especially [name]. Help me pray for everyone. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 30 — By This Everyone Will Know
fields.body_html:
“A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”

— John 13:34–35 (BSB)

How can people tell that someone is a follower of Jesus?

You might think it’s by the cross necklace they wear. Or by the fact that they go to church. Or by how many Bible verses they know. Those things are good. But Jesus gave a different answer.

On the night before He died, Jesus sat at supper with His disciples, just after washing their feet. And He gave them a new commandment: “Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.”

The commandment to love wasn’t new. But the standard was: “As I have loved you.” Not just love like normal people love. Love the way Jesus loves. Serving, sacrificing, forgiving, patient, kind. The kind of love that washes feet and goes to the cross.

Then Jesus said, “By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.” Love is how the world will recognize us. It’s like a family resemblance. When people see Christians loving each other and loving others the way Jesus does, they’ll say, Those people must belong to Jesus.

Look back at this whole book. That’s what we’ve been learning for 30 days. How to love your parents, your siblings and your family. How to be a true friend, choose friends wisely and welcome people who are left out. How to forgive, make peace, say sorry and even love your enemies. How to be part of God’s family at church, using your gifts, honoring older people, welcoming younger ones and carrying each other’s burdens. And how to love the whole world: every nation, the least of these, and everyone who hasn’t heard about Jesus yet.

It’s a lot! And none of us does it perfectly. But remember where love comes from: “As I have loved you.” You can love others because Jesus has loved you first. His love fills you up, like water filling roots, and then it flows out through your branches to everyone around you.

That’s what it means to branch out.

Think about it: Which day of this book challenged you most? What’s one person you want to love better because of it?

Try this: Look back at the tree you drew on Day 1. Add any new names to the branches. Then do one loving thing for someone on your tree today.

Dear Jesus, thank You for loving me so much. Help me love others the way You have loved me. Let my love for others show the world that I belong to You. Keep filling me with Your love, so it flows out to everyone around me. In Your name, Amen.

By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.” — John 13:34–35 (BSB) How can people tell that someone is a follower of Jesus? You might think it’s by the cross necklace they wear. Or by the fact that they go to church. Or by how many Bible verses they know. Those things are good. But Jesus gave a different answer. On the night before He died, Jesus sat at supper with His disciples, just after washing their feet. And He gave them a new commandment: “Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.” The commandment to love wasn’t new. But the standard was: “As I have loved you.” Not just love like normal people love. Love the way Jesus loves. Serving, sacrificing, forgiving, patient, kind. The kind of love that washes feet and goes to the cross. Then Jesus said, “By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.” Love is how the world will recognize us. It’s like a family resemblance. When people see Christians loving each other and loving others the way Jesus does, they’ll say, Those people must belong to Jesus. Look back at this whole book. That’s what we’ve been learning for 30 days. How to love your parents, your siblings and your family. How to be a true friend, choose friends wisely and welcome people who are left out. How to forgive, make peace, say sorry and even love your enemies. How to be part of God’s family at church, using your gifts, honoring older people, welcoming younger ones and carrying each other’s burdens. And how to love the whole world: every nation, the least of these, and everyone who hasn’t heard about Jesus yet. It’s a lot! And none of us does it perfectly. But remember where love comes from: “As I have loved you.” You can love others because Jesus has loved you first. His love fills you up, like water filling roots, and then it flows out through your branches to everyone around you. That’s what it means to branch out. Think about it: Which day of this book challenged you most? What’s one person you want to love better because of it? Try this: Look back at the tree you drew on Day 1. Add any new names to the branches. Then do one loving thing for someone on your tree today. Dear Jesus, thank You for loving me so much. Help me love others the way You have loved me. Let my love for others show the world that I belong to You. Keep filling me with Your love, so it flows out to everyone around me. In Your name, Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion: A Tree That Gives Shade
fields.body_html:
What a journey! For 30 days, you’ve been learning how God’s love branches out through you.

You started with the two greatest commandments: love God and love your neighbor. Roots going down, branches reaching out.

You learned about love at home: honoring your parents, living in harmony with your brothers and sisters, serving your family, listening when your parents say no and helping make your home a place where God is honored.

You learned about friends: being a friend who loves at all times, being loyal like Jonathan, walking with the wise, outdoing others in kindness, remembering that God sees you when you feel left out, and welcoming people on the edges.

You learned about forgiveness and peace: forgiving seventy-seven times, forgiving as the Lord forgave you, making things right, being a peacemaker, loving your enemies (while staying safe) and overcoming evil with good.

You learned about God’s family: being part of the body of Christ, using your gifts, honoring older people, welcoming younger kids, carrying each other’s burdens, and rejoicing and weeping together.

And you learned about loving the world: God’s family from every nation, serving the least of these, being ready to share your hope, telling your story and praying for everyone.

That’s a big, beautiful tree with branches reaching in every direction!

If you haven’t trusted Jesus yet

All of this love starts with God’s love for you. If you haven’t trusted Jesus yet, you can today. God loves you so much that He sent Jesus to die for your sins and rise again. You can pray something like this:

Dear Jesus, thank You for loving me so much. I know I have sinned, and I’m sorry. I believe You died for me and rose again. I trust You as my Savior, and I want to follow You as my Lord. Fill me with Your love, so I can love others. Amen.

If you prayed that, tell a parent, a pastor or another Christian you trust. They’ll want to celebrate with you!

What’s next

A healthy tree does one more thing: it bears fruit that feeds others, year after year, season after season.

In Book 6, the last book of Rooted, you’ll discover God’s purpose for your life: the good works He has planned for you, the gifts and time He’s given you, how to lead by serving, and how to finish well. And you’ll look ahead to the day Jesus comes back and everything is made new.

Until then, keep your roots deep in God, and keep your branches reaching out in love.

“And may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else.”

— 1 Thessalonians 3:12 (BSB)
